summary: Suggests a method for workstations to access mail dynamically from a mailbox server. It is a modified version of the IMAP2 definition in RFC 1064 and was published as an Experimental protocol. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: Instead of downloading all your letters, you read them at the post office. This was one early version of that idea.

questions: how is imap3 different from imap2
what are solicited and unsolicited responses in imap
subtitle: A counter-proposal to extend IMAP2 so workstations can read mail that stays on a server, with version and feature negotiation built in.

tldr.problem: Workstations make poor places to receive mail, and the existing IMAP2 protocol (RFC 1064) was seen by the author as too weak, with a muddled idea of which server data was requested and which was not.
tldr.mechanism: IMAP3 keeps the mailbox on a server and lets the client read and change it with tagged commands. It separates solicited from unsolicited data, adds a way to negotiate protocol versions and features, and lets the client see read-only status and create flags.
tldr.outcome: It was published as an Experimental protocol for the Internet community and is now Historic. It obsoleted RFC 1064.

today: RFC 1203 is marked Historic. It obsoleted RFC 1064 (IMAP2), and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC itself was published as an Experimental protocol.

sections.title: Why IMAP3 Was Written
sections.content:
RFC 1203 describes the Interactive Mail Access Protocol, Version 3 (IMAP3). Its goal is to let a possibly unreliable workstation read electronic mail from a reliable mailbox server, which the RFC calls a repository, in an efficient way.

The document says it is a modified version of RFC 1064, the IMAP2 definition. It was written as a counter-proposal to RFC 1176, which also proposed changes to IMAP2. The author objects that RFC 1176 adds little power, keeps a flawed notion of solicited and unsolicited data, lets the server assume things about the client's cache, offers optional features with no way to negotiate them, and assumes TCP/IP.

IMAP3 aims to stay upwards compatible with IMAP2 where it can. Every IMAP3 server is expected to behave like IMAP2 by default, so existing IMAP2 clients keep working.
sections.eli5: Some people disagreed about how to improve an older mail-reading system. The author wrote a different plan that fixes what they saw as mistakes while still working with old programs.

sections.title: Mail Lives on a Server, Not the Workstation
sections.content:
The RFC argues against delivering mail straight to each workstation. A workstation may be too busy to receive mail, may be out of service after a hardware failure, makes addresses hard to track when each person is tied to one machine, and is hard to keep up to date with complex mail protocols across many kinds of machines.

Instead, a mail server holds the mailbox and the workstation, called the client, reaches it through mail transactions. The same user can read mail from different clients at different times, and several users can open the same mailbox at once.

IMAP3 is described as a functional superset of POP2 (RFC 937). Unlike POP2 it can search and parse messages on the server, so a client does not have to download a whole mailbox. It handles reading mail only; sending is left to a mail transfer protocol such as SMTP (RFC 821). The RFC also contrasts IMAP3 with the DMSP protocol of PCMAIL (RFC 1056): in IMAP all mailbox state stays on the server and the client keeps nothing between connections.
sections.eli5: Keeping your mail on a big, careful computer is like keeping valuables in a bank vault instead of in your messy backpack. You can still look at them from any desk.

sections.title: Mailboxes as Keys and Values
sections.content:
IMAP is a mailbox access protocol, not a way to manipulate mail files. The RFC says nothing about how a server stores mail, and mailbox names other than the reserved INBOX depend on the operating system.

In the IMAP3 view a mailbox maps keys to values. There are three kinds of key. Generic keys are mail-format independent names such as TO. Canonical keys such as $TO let the server gather related values; in an RFC 822 message the server could build $TO from the To, Resent-To, Apparently-To and CC fields. Concrete keys name a format-specific field, such as APPARENTLY-TO, and return NIL if no such field exists.

The predefined generic keys are BCC, BODY, CC, FROM, HEADER, SIZE, SUBJECT, TEXT and TO. The canonical keys are $CC, $FROM, $SUBJECT and $TO. The RFC calls this concept experimental and expects IMAP to move away from its reliance on RFC 822 so it can handle things like multi-media mail.
sections.eli5: Think of each letter as a filing card with labelled boxes, like From and Subject. You can ask for the contents of any box by its label, and you get a blank answer if that box does not exist.

sections.title: Tagged Commands and Responses
sections.content:
A client command begins with a unique tag such as A0001, and the server marks its reply with the same tag. Data the server sends because of a request is solicited and carries that tag. Data the server sends on its own is unsolicited and carries the tag *. All solicited data must arrive before the command's completion response, so the client knows it has everything. The server may handle several requests in any order, which lets it run slow searches in the background.

A normal session is: greeting, LOGIN, SELECT a mailbox, FETCH data, STORE changes, EXPUNGE to remove messages flagged \DELETED, then LOGOUT. Other commands include NOOP, CHECK, COPY, SEARCH, BBOARD, FIND, READONLY, READWRITE, FLAGS and SET.FLAGS.

FETCH returns three kinds of data. FAST expands to (FLAGS INTERNALDATE RFC822.SIZE). ALL adds the parsed ENVELOPE, a structured list of date, subject, from, sender, reply-to, to, cc, bcc, in-reply-to and message-id. The third kind is the message itself: RFC822.HEADER, RFC822.TEXT or RFC822. SEARCH can combine criteria and negate any of them with a ~ prefix, and the server can send unsolicited SEARCH results, for example to announce new mail.

The response codes are OK, NO and BAD for success, failure and a protocol bug, and BYE before the server closes the connection. A + response tells the client the server is ready for a literal, which keeps client and server in step.
sections.eli5: Every question you ask gets a numbered ticket, and the answer comes back with the same number. The server can also tap you on the shoulder with news, like new mail, and those taps are marked with a star.

sections.title: Negotiating Versions and Features
sections.content:
Servers must behave exactly as IMAP2 (RFC 1064) unless the client asks otherwise. SUPPORTED.VERSIONS asks which protocol versions and features the server offers. SELECT.VERSION picks one, for example (3 0), and SELECT.FEATURES picks features; each feature has an inverse written with a ~ prefix. Asking for something the server does not support gets a NO. SELECT.VERSION is an error once a mailbox has been selected, and the default version is 2.0.

The appendix lists example features. Required ones are AUTO.SET.SEEN (default disabled), which sets the \SEEN flag as a side effect of fetching the message body, and TAGGED.SOLICITED (default enabled for IMAP3, disabled in IMAP2 mode), which tags solicited replies with the client's tag instead of the asterisk tag. Recommended ones include EIGHT.BIT.TRANSPARENT and NEW.MAIL.NOTIFY, and an optional SEND feature adds a command for the server to send mail.

IMAP3 also adds ways to learn whether a mailbox is read-only (READONLY and READWRITE) and to create or delete user flags (SET.FLAGS).
sections.eli5: Before you start talking, you and the server compare lists of what each of you can do and agree on the rules. If you say nothing, you both use the old, familiar rules.

sections.title: Implementations, Syntax and Security
sections.content:
The RFC reports that SUMEX had IMAP2 clients for Xerox and TI Explorer Lisp machines, a portable C client library and a Macintosh client, along with IMAP2 servers for TOPS-20 and 4.2/3 BSD Unix. It lists several other client platforms, and says the specification sets no formal size limits though some servers have them. It closes with a formal syntax in augmented BNF and a sample session.

Over TCP the server listens on port 220; over CHAOS it listens for the contact name IMAP3. The protocol uses ASCII. Its security section says only that security issues are not discussed. The LOGIN command sends the user name and password as plain arguments.
sections.eli5: The paper describes the programs that already worked and the exact grammar to follow. It does not talk about keeping secrets, and passwords are sent as ordinary words.
